newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: AMLC Beef Weekly - Australian export prices.
newsitem.headline: AMLC Beef Weekly - Australian export prices.

text.p: Australian Meat and Livestock Corp's (AMLC) weekly export prices are as follows:
AUSTRALIAN EXPORT PRICES TO U.S. IN U.S. CENTS/LB, CIF.
Bull (95 Chemical Lean) 87 n/c on last week
Shank (90 CL) 81 +2
Trimmings (85 CL) 72 +2
Chucks (85 CL) 73 -1
AUSTRALIAN EXPORT PRICES TO JAPAN IN U.S. CENTS/LB CIF.
Chilled grassfed fullsets 122 -1 on last week
Chilled grassfed loin:striploin 173 -3
cube roll 230 -5
tender loin 435 -5

AMLC COMMENTARY: Cattle prices held firm this week, assisted by an across-the-board reduction in supplies as a result of a holiday-shortened week.

Yardings in surveyed centres fell by 30 percent to about 14,000 head in both New South Wales and Queensland, and by 20 percent in Victoria to 7,300 head. Numbers were also down substantially in South Australia and Western Australia.

In export markets, manufacturing beef prices improved, but demand for non-manufacturing beef items was weaker. This may mark the beginning of a period of contrasting price movements between these markets. Manufacturing beef supplies are expected
to tighten across the Pacific Rim, while heavier supplies of cattle out of U.S. feedlots are expected to increase availability of fed beef in these markets.

In the U.S. this week, smaller supplies from New Zealand and a moderation in product from Australia led to a firming in prices of lean imported product. These price rises were enhanced by a weakening Australian dollar.
Imported manufacturing beef prices rose across the entire product range by one to 12 cents per kg. The greatest price rises were in trimmings and the leaner end of items offered.

Wholesale market values of beef in Japan declined by between 20 yen a kg and 40 yen a kg across the range of both U.S. and Australian product. Poor Japanese beef consumption levels and a strong yen are seen as the primary reasons for the deterioration in beef export prices to Japan this year. With the recent easing in the yen now translating into cheaper beef prices to Japanese consumers, it is hoped that the consumption slide can be arrested.
There is still a large difference between export beef prices and prices of beef on the Japanese wholesale market.

Non-manufacturing beef prices were also easier in the U.S. this week, with boxed beef values falling to 98.8 US cents a pound, their lowest level since February 18. Although the numbers of lot-fed cattle being marketed has increased in recent weeks compared with April levels, slaughterings fell in the week. This may be the first sign that feedlots in the U.S. are becoming less current and are falling behind in marketing cattle.

If U.S. cattlemen resist marketing cattle, numbers and weights will rise in unison, bolstering production levels and placing the U.S. beef complex under even further pressure. If this unfolds it could set back the recovery in beef and cattle prices until early 1998.
Among important developoments in the Americas over the past week, Argentina and Parguay have been declared foot and mouth disease free after vaccination.
And McDonalds' has admitted that its 55 US cents hamburger promotion has been a failure.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
